rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Jacob says he discloses his deepest grief only to God; bathth is the most intense grief, named because its bearer cannot contain it and must reveal it.
rows.anchor: والبث: أشد الحزن، سمي بذلك لأن صاحبه لا يصبر عليه حتى يثبته أي يظهره

rows.speaker: الحسن
rows.claim: Hasan glosses Jacob’s bathth as his need.
rows.anchor: قال الحسن: بثي أي: حاجتي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A neighbor asks why Jacob has withered before his father’s age; Jacob attributes it to the trial of grief over Joseph, then repents after God asks why he complains to creatures, and God forgives him.
rows.anchor: يا يعقوب أتشكوني إلى خلقي؟ فقال: يا رب خطيئة أخطأتها فاغفرها لي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Asked what took his sight and bent his back, Jacob says weeping for Joseph and grief for his brother did so; God withholds relief until Jacob supplicates.
rows.anchor: أذهب بصري بكائي على يوسف، وقوس ظهري حزني على أخيه. فأوحى الله إليه: أتشكوني؟

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God promises to restore even dead sons, but reproaches Jacob’s household for withholding sheep from a poor visitor; prophets and then the poor are most beloved, so Jacob is told to feed the poor.
rows.anchor: لو كانا ميتين لأخرجتهما لك، وإنما وجدت عليكم لأنكم ذبحتم شاة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Afterward Jacob regularly invites poor people to share his midday and evening meals.
rows.anchor: فكان يتغدى ويتعشى مع المساكين

rows.speaker: وهب بن منبه
rows.claim: Wahb says God explained Jacob’s eighty-year loss of Joseph as punishment for roasting a young goat, restricting his neighbor’s food, and eating without feeding him.
rows.anchor: وعن وهب بن منبه قال: أوحى الله تعالى إلى يعقوب: أتدري لم عاقبتك وحبست عنك يوسف ثمانين سنة؟

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another report says Jacob’s affliction began when he slaughtered a calf before its lowing mother.
rows.anchor: وروي: أن سبب ابتلاء يعقوب أنه ذبح عجلا بين يدي أمه وهي تخور

rows.speaker: وهب والسدي وغيرهما
rows.claim: Wahb, al-Suddi, and others report that Gabriel visited Joseph in prison and asked whether he recognized him; Joseph saw a pure form with a pleasant fragrance.
rows.anchor: وقال وهب والسدي وغيرهما: أتى جبريل يوسف عليه السلام في السجن فقال: هل تعرفني

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Jacob knows from God what others do not: that Joseph is alive.
rows.anchor: يعني: أعلم من حياة يوسف ما لا تعلمون

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: When the Angel of Death says he did not take Joseph’s soul, Jacob is reassured and hopes to see Joseph again.
rows.anchor: قال: لا فسكن يعقوب وطمع في رؤيته

rows.speaker: السدي
rows.claim: After hearing his sons describe the Egyptian ruler, Jacob’s hope stirs and he suspects the ruler may be Joseph, so he sends them to search for Joseph and his brother.
rows.anchor: وقال السدي: لما أخبره ولده بسيرة الملك أحست نفس يعقوب وطمع وقال لعله يوسف

rows.speaker: عبد الله بن يزيد بن أبي فروة
rows.claim: In a letter to Joseph while Benjamin is detained, Jacob recounts his family’s trials, Joseph’s disappearance and bloodied shirt, his lost sight, and protests that his family neither steals nor raises thieves; unless Benjamin is returned he will pray against Joseph’s descendants, prompting Joseph to weep and reveal himself.
rows.anchor: وروي عن عبد الله بن يزيد بن أبي فروة: أن يعقوب عليه السلام كتب كتابا إلى يوسف عليه السلام حين حبس بنيامين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Taḥassus means investigating and seeking news by the senses; it is close to tajassus, except the ḥāʾ form is used for good and the jīm form for evil.
rows.anchor: والتحسس بالحاء والجيم لا يبعد أحدهما من الآخر، إلا أن التحسس بالحاء في الخير وبالجيم في الشر

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas says God’s rawḥ here means God’s mercy.
rows.anchor: قال ابن عباس: معناه التمسوا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another gloss takes God’s rawḥ to mean relief.
rows.anchor: وقيل: من فرج الله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The narrative omits the return journey: the brothers went back toward Egypt and entered upon Joseph.
rows.anchor: وفيه إضمار تقديره: فخرجوا راجعين إلى مصر حتى وصلوا إليها فدخلوا على يوسف

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The harm affecting the family was hardship and hunger.
rows.anchor: قالوا يا أيها العزيز مسنا وأهلنا الضر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The offered merchandise was small, poor, and unmarketable, accepted only through the seller’s indulgence; izjaʾ originally means driving or pushing, and it is called that because it does not sell and is taken only reluctantly.
rows.anchor: وأصل الإزجاء: السوق والدفع. وقيل: للبضاعة مزجاة لأنها غير نافقة

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas identifies the merchandise as debased counterfeit dirhams.
rows.anchor: فقال ابن عباس: كانت دراهم رديئة زيوفا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One reported identification is worn sacks and ropes.
rows.anchor: وقيل: كانت خلق الغرائر والحبال

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another identification is Bedouin goods made of wool and dried curd.
rows.anchor: وقيل: كانت من متاع الأعراب من الصوف والأقط

rows.speaker: الكلبي ومقاتل
rows.claim: Al-Kalbi and Muqatil identify the merchandise as green grain.
rows.anchor: وقال الكلبي ومقاتل: كانت الحبة الخضراء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another reported identification is flour made from colocynth seeds.
rows.anchor: وقيل: كانت من سويق المقل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another reported identification is hides and sandals.
rows.anchor: وقيل: كانت الأدم والنعال

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: They ask Joseph to give them the full measure he previously gave when they paid with good money.
rows.anchor: أي: أعطنا ما كنت تعطينا قبل بالثمن الجيد الوافي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Most exegetes understand “be charitable to us” as asking Joseph to favor them by accepting the difference between good and inferior payment without reducing their measure.
rows.anchor: هذا قول أكثر المفسرين

rows.speaker: ابن جريج والضحاك
rows.claim: Ibn Jurayj and al-Dahhak instead take the plea for charity to mean asking Joseph to return their brother.
rows.anchor: وقال ابن جريج والضحاك: وتصدق علينا برد أخينا إلينا

rows.speaker: الضحاك
rows.claim: Al-Dahhak says they did not say “may God reward you” because they did not know Joseph was a believer.
rows.anchor: وقال الضحاك: لم يقولوا إن الله يجزيك؛ لأنهم لم يعلموا أنه مؤمن

rows.speaker: سفيان بن عيينة
rows.claim: Sufyan ibn ʿUyayna uses this verse to argue that charity was lawful for prophets besides Muhammad, since Joseph’s brothers ask him for charity.
rows.anchor: فقال سفيان: ألم تسمع قوله تعالى

rows.speaker: الحسن
rows.claim: Hasan corrects someone who says “God, be charitable to me”: God does not give charity in pursuit of reward, so one should ask Him to give or show favor.
rows.anchor: قال: إن الله لا يتصدق وإنما يتصدق من يبغي الثواب، قل: اللهم أعطني أو تفضل علي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The brothers apologize, acknowledging that God preferred Joseph and that their treatment of him was sinful; khatiʾ is deliberate error, while akhtaʾ is inadvertent error.
rows.anchor: يقال: خطئ خطئا إذا تعمد، وأخطأ إذا كان غير متعمد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Joseph is forbearing: he tells them there will be no reproach or reminder of their sin from that day onward, and asks God to forgive them.
rows.anchor: لا تعيير عليكم اليوم، ولا أذكر لكم ذنبكم بعد اليوم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: After identifying himself, Joseph asks after his father; when told Jacob lost his sight, he gives them his shirt.
rows.anchor: فلما عرفهم يوسف نفسه سألهم عن أبيه، فقال: ما فعل أبي بعدي؟

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The shirt will make Jacob see again; another reading of the instruction is that Jacob should come to Joseph with sight restored, since Joseph had invited him.
rows.anchor: وقيل: يأتيني بصيرا لأنه كان قد دعاه

rows.speaker: الحسن
rows.claim: Hasan says Joseph did not know Jacob would regain sight until God informed him.
rows.anchor: قال الحسن: لم يعلم أنه يعود بصيرا إلا بعد أن أعلمه الله

rows.speaker: الضحاك
rows.claim: Al-Dahhak says the shirt was woven in Paradise.
rows.anchor: وقال الضحاك: كان ذلك القميص من نسج الجنة

rows.speaker: مجاهد
rows.claim: Mujahid reports Gabriel ordered Joseph to send Abraham’s Paradise-silk shirt: inherited by Isaac and Jacob, it was kept as Joseph’s protective amulet, placed on him when he was naked in the well, and later sent to Jacob because its paradisal scent heals the sick and afflicted.
rows.anchor: وعن مجاهد قال: أمره جبريل أن يرسل إليه قميصه، وكان ذلك القميص قميص إبراهيم عليه السلام

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Jacob’s grandchildren think Joseph is dead and regard Jacob’s continued remembrance as his old error of straying from what is right.
rows.anchor: والضلال هو الذهاب عن طريق الصواب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The herald is the bearer of news from Joseph; Ibn Masʿud says he came ahead of the caravan.
rows.anchor: قال ابن مسعود: جاء البشير بين يدي العير

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas identifies the herald as Judah.
rows.anchor: قال ابن عباس: هو يهوذا

rows.speaker: السدي
rows.claim: Al-Suddi says Judah volunteered to carry the shirt: he had once brought Jacob the bloodstained shirt and news of Joseph’s supposed death, and now would bring glad news that Joseph lived.
rows.anchor: قال [السدي: قال يهوذا] (1)

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas says Judah carried the shirt barefoot and bareheaded, running with seven loaves that were not finished before reaching Jacob after an eighty-parasang journey.
rows.anchor: قال ابن عباس: حمله يهوذا وخرج حافيا حاسرا يعدو ومعه سبعة أرغفة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another report names the herald as Malik ibn Dhʿar.
rows.anchor: وقيل: البشير مالك بن ذعر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Dalal means straying from the path of correctness.
rows.anchor: والضلال هو الذهاب عن طريق الصواب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The herald lays Joseph’s shirt on Jacob’s face, restoring his sight, strength, youth, and joy after blindness, weakness, old age, and grief.
rows.anchor: ألقى البشير قميص يوسف على وجه يعقوب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Jacob’s claim that he knows what others do not refers to his knowledge that Joseph lived and that God would reunite them.
rows.anchor: من حياة يوسف وأن الله يجمع بيننا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: When Jacob asks about Joseph, the herald says Joseph is Egypt’s king and a Muslim; Jacob says the blessing is now complete.
rows.anchor: قال: الآن تمت النعمة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The brothers call themselves sinners.
rows.anchor: {قالوا يا أبانا استغفر لنا ذنوبنا إنا كنا خاطئين} مذنبين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Most exegetes say Jacob delayed his prayer until predawn, the time when God calls for supplicants; after praying he asks forgiveness for his anguish and impatience over Joseph and for his sons’ wrong against Joseph, and God reveals that He forgave them all.
rows.anchor: قال أكثر المفسرين: أخر الدعاء إلى السحر

rows.speaker: عكرمة عن ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ikrima, transmitting from Ibn Abbas, says “I shall seek forgiveness” means on Friday night.
rows.anchor: وعن عكرمة عن ابن عباس رضي الله عنهما: سوف أستغفر لكم

rows.speaker: وهب
rows.claim: Wahb says Jacob sought forgiveness for them every Friday night for more than twenty years.
rows.anchor: قال وهب: كان يستغفر لهم كل

rows.speaker: طاوس
rows.claim: Tawus says Jacob delayed until predawn on Friday night, which coincided with the night of Ashura.
rows.anchor: وقال طاوس: أخر الدعاء إلى السحر من ليلة الجمعة

rows.speaker: الشعبي
rows.claim: Al-Shaʿbi says Jacob delayed asking God until he had asked Joseph to pardon his brothers.
rows.anchor: وعن الشعبي قال: سوف أستغفر لكم ربي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Joseph sent the herald with two hundred camels and much equipment; Jacob’s party set out for Egypt, numbering seventy-two men and women, though Masruq says ninety-three.
rows.anchor: فخرجوا وهم اثنان وسبعون من بين رجل وامرأة. وقال مسروق: كانوا ثلاثة وتسعين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: As Jacob approaches Egypt, Joseph and the king above him ride out with four thousand soldiers and Egyptians to welcome him; Jacob leans on Judah, mistakes the approaching ruler for Pharaoh, and learns it is his son.
rows.anchor: فخرج يوسف والملك في أربعة آلاف من الجنود وركب أهل مصر معهما يتلقون يعقوب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: As Joseph moves to greet Jacob first, Gabriel says Jacob must greet first; Jacob then greets Joseph as the remover of sorrows.
rows.anchor: فقال جبريل: لا حتى يبدأ يعقوب بالسلام، فقال يعقوب: السلام عليك يا مذهب الأحزان

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Most exegetes identify Joseph’s parents as Jacob and his maternal aunt Leah, since his mother Rachel died giving birth to Benjamin.
rows.anchor: قال أكثر المفسرين: هو أبوه وخالته ليا، وكانت أمه راحيل قد ماتت في نفاس بنيامين

rows.speaker: الحسن
rows.claim: Hasan says the parents were Jacob and Joseph’s mother, who was still alive.
rows.anchor: وقال الحسن: هو أبوه وأمه، وكانت حية

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Some commentaries say God revived Joseph’s mother so that she came with Jacob to Egypt.
rows.anchor: وفي بعض التفاسير أن الله عز وجل أحيا أمه حتى جاءت مع يعقوب إلى مصر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: To explain how Joseph says “enter Egypt” after they have entered, one view places his words at the earlier meeting before they crossed into Egypt.
rows.anchor: قيل: إن يوسف إنما قال لهم هذا القول حين تلقاهم قبل دخولهم مصر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another explanation takes the passage as having reordered clauses and attaches “if God wills” to Jacob’s promise to seek forgiveness.
rows.anchor: وفي الآية تقديم وتأخير، والاستثناء يرجع إلى الاستغفار

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another view attaches the exception to safety from an entry permit: people formerly entered Egypt only with a ruler’s permit, and Joseph promises security without one; the wording is compared to the promise in 48:27.
rows.anchor: وقيل: الاستثناء يرجع إلى الأمن من الجواز

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A further view reads in as idh, “when,” so the phrase means “when God willed”; 3:139 is similarly glossed “when you are believers.”
rows.anchor: وقيل: " إن " ها هنا بمعنى إذ

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Joseph seats his parents on the throne, a raised seat.
rows.anchor: الرفع: هو النقل إلى العلو

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Those who prostrate are Jacob, Joseph’s aunt, and his brothers; the greeting of that era was prostration understood as bowing and humility, not placing foreheads on the ground.
rows.anchor: وكانت تحية الناس يومئذ السجود، ولم يرد بالسجود وضع الجباه على الأرض

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another view says they placed their foreheads on the ground as greeting and veneration rather than worship, a practice permitted in earlier communities and abrogated by Islamic law.
rows.anchor: وقيل: وضعوا الجباه على الأرض وكان ذلك على طريق التحية والتعظيم، لا على طريق العبادة

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas interprets the prostration as their prostrating to God before Joseph; the author judges the first explanation more sound.
rows.anchor: عن ابن عباس أنه قال: معناه: خروا لله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Joseph says the family’s prostration fulfills his earlier dream of eleven stars, the sun, and moon bowing to him.
rows.anchor: وهو قوله: "إني رأيت أحد عشر كوكبا والشمس والقمر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Joseph says God favored him by taking him from prison, not the more grievous pit, out of courtesy so he would not shame his brothers after forgiving them; release from prison brought kingship, whereas the pit led to enslavement, and the pit followed their envy while prison repaid his own lapse.
rows.anchor: ولم يقل من الجب مع كونه أشد بلاء من السجن، استعمالا للكرم، لكيلا يخجل إخوته

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The badw is open country inhabited by herders and their livestock; badā means to go out to the countryside.
rows.anchor: بسيط من الأرض يسكنه أهل المواشي بماشيتهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Satan stirred division between Joseph and his brothers through envy.
rows.anchor: أفسد، {الشيطان بيني وبين إخوتي}

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Latif means possessing subtle kindness and, in one gloss, kindness toward whomever God wills; truly, it is one who delivers beneficence gently.
rows.anchor: إن ربي لطيف} أي: ذو لطف

rows.speaker: أهل التاريخ
rows.claim: Historians say Jacob lived twenty-four happy, comfortable years in Egypt, died there, and was carried by Joseph for burial beside Isaac in Syria.
rows.anchor: قال أهل التاريخ: أقام يعقوب بمصر عند يوسف أربعا وعشرين سنة في أغبط حال وأهنأ عيش

rows.speaker: سعيد بن جبير
rows.claim: Saʿid ibn Jubayr says Jacob was moved in a teak coffin to Jerusalem and buried in one grave with his twin Esau, who died that day; each lived 147 years.
rows.anchor: قال سعيد بن جبير: نقل يعقوب عليه السلام في تابوت من ساج إلى بيت المقدس

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Because worldly enjoyment does not last even after God reunites Joseph’s family, Joseph asks God for a good final outcome.
rows.anchor: على أن نعيم الدنيا لا يدوم سأل الله تعالى حسن العاقبة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Joseph thanks God for Egypt’s rule and for teaching dream interpretation; he invokes God as creator of heaven and earth, his helper and manager in both lives, asks to die Muslim, and to join his prophet forebears.
rows.anchor: والملك: اتساع المقدور لمن له السياسة والتدبير

rows.speaker: قتادة
rows.claim: Qatada says no prophet besides Joseph ever asked God for death.
rows.anchor: قال قتادة: لم يسأل نبي من الأنبياء الموت إلا يوسف

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The narrative says Joseph yearned for his Lord after God reunited his family and brought his parents and household to him, so he made this prayer.
rows.anchor: لما جمع الله شمله وأوصل إليه أبويه وأهله اشتاق إلى ربه عز وجل

rows.speaker: الحسن
rows.claim: Hasan says Joseph lived many years after this prayer; another account says he died within a week.
rows.anchor: قال الحسن: عاش بعد هذا سنين كثيرة. وقال غيره: لما قال هذا القول لم يمض عليه أسبوع

rows.speaker: الكلبي
rows.claim: Al-Kalbi says Joseph was absent from his father for twenty-two years; another report says forty.
rows.anchor: فقال الكلبي: اثنتان وعشرون سنة. وقيل: أربعون سنة

rows.speaker: الحسن
rows.claim: Hasan says Joseph entered the well aged seventeen, was absent from Jacob for eighty years, lived twenty-three years after reunion, and died aged 120.
rows.anchor: وقال الحسن: ألقي يوسف في الجب وهو ابن سبع عشرة سنة، وغاب عن أبيه ثمانين سنة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Torah gives Joseph’s age at death as 110 and says he had Ephraim, Misha, and Rahmah, Job’s afflicted wife, by al-ʿUzayr’s wife.
rows.anchor: وفي التوراة مات وهو ابن مائة وعشر سنين، وولد ليوسف من امرأة العزير ثلاثة أولاد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Other accounts say Joseph lived sixty years after his father or even longer; reports on his lifespan differ.
rows.anchor: وقيل: عاش يوسف بعد أبيه ستين سنة. وقيل: أكثر. واختلفت الأقاويل فيه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One account says Joseph died at 120 and was put in a marble chest in the Nile because Egyptians disputed where to bury him, each hoping for his blessing; they chose the Nile so its branches would carry blessing throughout Egypt.
rows.anchor: فدفنوه في النيل في صندوق من رخام، وذلك أنه لما مات تشاح الناس فيه

rows.speaker: عكرمة
rows.claim: Ikrima says burial on the Nile’s east bank made that side fertile and the west barren; moving Joseph west reversed the result, so he was buried midstream, where both sides prospered, until Moses later took him to the ancestral burial place in Syria.
rows.anchor: وقال عكرمة: دفن في الجانب الأيمن

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The revelation is hidden news about Jacob’s sons: Muhammad was not present when they resolved to throw Joseph into the well and plotted against him.
rows.anchor: ما كنت يا محمد عند أولاد يعقوب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Most people will not believe even if Muhammad eagerly wishes them to believe.
rows.anchor: يا محمد، {ولو حرصت بمؤمنين}

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Jews and Quraysh asked Muhammad for Joseph’s story; though he told it in agreement with the Torah they did not believe, and the Prophet grieved until told that his effort would not make most people believe.
rows.anchor: وروي أن اليهود وقريشا سألوا رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم عن قصة يوسف

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Muhammad asks no payment for conveying the message and calling people to God; the Quran is a reminder and admonition for all worlds.
rows.anchor: على تبليغ الرسالة والدعاء إلى الله تعالى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: People pass many signs in heaven and earth but turn away, neither reflecting nor learning from them.
rows.anchor: لا يتفكرون فيها ولا يعتبرون بها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Many acknowledge God as creator of heaven and earth and sender of rain, yet still worship idols and associate partners with Him.
rows.anchor: قالوا: الله، ثم مع ذلك يعبدون الأصنام

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas says the verse concerns pagan Arabs’ talbiya, in which they proclaimed no partner for God except a partner whom God owned along with what that partner owned.
rows.anchor: وعن ابن عباس أنه قال: إنها نزلت في تلبية المشركين من العرب

rows.speaker: عطاء
rows.claim: Ata says it concerns supplication: unbelievers forget God in ease but pray to Him sincerely in affliction, as described at 10:22 and 29:65.
rows.anchor: وقال عطاء: هذا في الدعاء، وذلك أن الكفار نسوا ربهم في الرخاء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A ghashiya is an enveloping punishment; Mujahid says punishment that covers them, comparing 29:55.
rows.anchor: أي: عقوبة مجللة. قال مجاهد: عذاب يغشاهم

rows.speaker: قتادة
rows.claim: Qatada glosses the threatened ghashiya as a calamity or assault.
rows.anchor: قال قتادة: وقيعة

rows.speaker: الضحاك
rows.claim: Al-Dahhak takes it to mean lightning bolts and calamities.
rows.anchor: وقال الضحاك: يعني الصواعق والقوارع

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas says the blast will strike people while they are in their marketplaces, unaware of the Hour.
rows.anchor: قال ابن عباس: تهيج الصيحة بالناس وهم في أسواقهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Prophet’s way is the invitation he makes and the path he follows.
rows.anchor: الدعوة التي أدعو إليها والطريقة التي أنا عليها

rows.speaker: مقاتل
rows.claim: Muqatil says “my way” means my religion, as in the call to the way of the Lord at 16:125.
rows.anchor: وقال مقاتل: ديني، نظيره قوله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Calling on clear insight means acting with certainty and knowledge that distinguishes truth from falsehood.
rows.anchor: على يقين. والبصيرة: هي المعرفة التي تميز بها بين الحق والباطل

rows.speaker: الكلبي وابن زيد
rows.claim: Al-Kalbi and Ibn Zayd say the Prophet and every believing follower summon people to God; followers must call to what he called and remind people through the Quran.
rows.anchor: هذا قول الكلبي وابن زيد، قالوا: حق على من اتبعه أن يدعو إلى ما دعا إليه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another syntactic reading ends the clause at “I call to God,” then says that both Muhammad and every follower stand upon insight from their Lord.
rows.anchor: ثم استأنف: {على بصيرة أنا ومن اتبعني}

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas praises Muhammad’s Companions as the best-guided people, a source of knowledge, storehouse of faith, and army of the Merciful.
rows.anchor: قال ابن عباس: يعني أصحاب محمد صلى الله عليه وسلم كانوا على أحسن طريقة

rows.speaker: عبد الله بن مسعود
rows.claim: Ibn Masʿud urges people to follow the deceased because the living may fall into temptation; Muhammad’s Companions were the best generation, purest-hearted, deepest in knowledge, least affected, chosen to establish the faith, and worthy of honor and emulation.
rows.anchor: قال عبد الله بن مسعود: من كان مستنا فليستن بمن قد مات

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Prophet is told to declare God transcendent above what people associate with Him and to disavow being one of the polytheists.
rows.anchor: أي: وقل سبحان الله تنزيها له عما أشركوا به

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God sent only human men as messengers, not angels; they received revelation.
rows.anchor: يا محمد، {إلا رجالا} لا ملائكة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Hafs reads nuhi with first-person nūn and a kasra on ḥāʾ, while the other readers read yūḥā with yāʾ and fatḥa on ḥāʾ.
rows.anchor: قرأ حفص: {نوحي} بالنون وكسر الحاء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The messengers were from towns rather than nomadic camps, because townspeople are more intelligent, virtuous, knowledgeable, and forbearing.
rows.anchor: من أهل الأمصار دون البوادي، لأن أهل الأمصار أعقل وأفضل وأعلم وأحلم

rows.speaker: الحسن
rows.claim: Hasan says God never sent a prophet from the nomads, jinn, or women.
rows.anchor: وقال الحسن: لم يبعث الله نبيا من بدو، ولا من الجن، ولا من النساء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another view says no prophet came from the Bedouins because they were coarse and harsh.
rows.anchor: من أهل البادية لغلظهم وجفائهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The deniers should travel the land and consider the end of earlier peoples who rejected their messengers.
rows.anchor: يعني: الأمم المكذبة فيعتبروا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God’s practice is to save His obedient allies when punishment descends; the afterlife abode is better for the God-fearing, with the omitted connection understood from context.
rows.anchor: هذا فعلنا بأهل ولايتنا وطاعتنا؛ أن ننجيهم عند نزول العذاب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One view understands dar al-akhira as “the abode of the final state.”
rows.anchor: قيل: معناه ولدار الحال الآخرة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another view treats “the abode of the Hereafter” as an expression adding a thing to itself, like “the truth of certainty” and weekday names; the closing “will you not reason?” is glossed as believing.
rows.anchor: وقيل: هو إضافة الشيء إلى نفسه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Kufans and Abu Jaʿfar read kudhibu with a light consonant, a reading ʿAʾisha rejected; the other readers double the consonant.
rows.anchor: فقرأ أهل الكوفة وأبو جعفر: {كذبوا} بالتخفيف وكانت عائشة تنكر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Those who double the consonant take it to mean the messengers despaired that their people would believe.
rows.anchor: فمن شدد قال: معناه حتى استيئس الرسل من إيمان قومهم

rows.speaker: مجاهد
rows.claim: Mujahid’s light reading qad kudhibu has two interpretations: the disbelievers thought the messengers lied, or the messengers knew their people had falsely claimed belief while persisting in unbelief.
rows.anchor: روي عن مجاهد أنه قرأ: وقد كذبوا بفتح الكاف والذال مخففة ولها تأويلان

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The messengers were certain their peoples had utterly rejected them, leaving no hope that they would believe; here ẓann means certainty, as Qatada also says.
rows.anchor: وظنوا: أي أيقنوا -يعني الرسل-

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another interpretation says the messengers despaired that the rejecters would believe and thought their own believers had renounced them under severe trial and delayed victory.
rows.anchor: وقال بعضهم: معناه: حتى إذا استيئس الرسل ممن كذبهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: On the light reading, the messengers despaired of their people believing, while the people thought the messengers had lied about the promised punishment.
rows.anchor: ومن قرأ بالتخفيف قال: معناه:

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas says the messengers’ hearts weakened: they thought the promise of victory had failed, being human and distressed by delay, then God’s help came; he links this to 2:214.
rows.anchor: وروي عن ابن عباس: معناه ضعف قلوب الرسل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The common reading of “we save whom We will” uses two nuns, an active verb, and makes “whom” accusative; Ibn ʿAmir, Hamza, ʿAsim, and Yaʿqub read one doubled nun in the passive, matching the written muṣḥaf and making “whom” nominative. Those saved at punishment are obedient believers.
rows.anchor: وقرأ ابن عامر وحمزة وعاصم ويعقوب بنون واحدة مضمومة وتشديد الجيم وفتح الياء على ما لم يسم فاعله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God’s punishment cannot be turned away from criminal people, meaning polytheists.
rows.anchor: {عن القوم المجرمين} يعني: المشركين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The account of Joseph and his brothers is an admonition for people of understanding; the Quran is not fabricated but confirms the Torah and Gospel, details what people need of lawful and unlawful matters and commands and prohibitions, and is guidance and mercy for believers.
rows.anchor: من التوراة والإنجيل {وتفصيل كل شيء}

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Subhan declares God wholly free of evil and deficiency, emphatically; it can also express amazement. Asra means to make someone travel by night, and the servant is Muhammad.
rows.anchor: سبحان الله: تنزيه الله تعالى من كل سوء، ووصفه بالبراءة من كل نقص على طريق المبالغة

rows.speaker: مالك بن صعصعة
rows.claim: The Prophet reports that Gabriel brought the Buraq to him while he was between sleep and wake in the Hijr of the Sacred Mosque; this is the beginning of the Miʿraj account.
rows.anchor: روى قتادة عن أنس عن مالك بن صعصعة أن رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم قال

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Some say the ascent began from Umm Hani’s house; “from the Sacred Mosque” can mean from the whole Meccan sanctuary.
rows.anchor: وقال قوم: عرج به من دار أم هانئ بنت أبي طالب

rows.speaker: مقاتل
rows.claim: Muqatil dates the Night Journey to a year before the Hijra; other reports place it in Rajab or Ramadan.
rows.anchor: قال مقاتل: كانت ليلة الإسراء قبل الهجرة بسنة، ويقال: كان في رجب
